name: Profound RF

chain: Firmer skin, softer wrinkles and scars
angle.text: Profound is discussed as a hardmaxxing option for skin laxity, wrinkles and acne scarring. It is documented mainly in registered device studies.

summary: Clinic-based radiofrequency microneedling system aimed at skin laxity, wrinkles and scars; documented mainly in registered device studies.
note: Specific results are not summarized from the available sources.
currentQuick:
Profound is a radiofrequency microneedling system performed in clinics. It is discussed as a way to address skin laxity, wrinkles and acne scars.
The available documentation is mostly trial registrations, including cellulite, wrinkle and acne-scar studies; outcome data are not covered here.
How it works: Microneedling punctures the skin with fine needles to trigger a healing response; RF devices add energy delivered through or beside the needles.
Risks and caveats: General microneedling concerns include infection risk when performed in unregulated settings, as reported by health officials in relation to related facial procedures. Device-specific safety findings are not summarized here.
deepLead:
Profound is a radiofrequency (RF) microneedling system used in aesthetic medicine. It combines needle insertion into the skin with RF energy delivered at depth, and is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a hardmaxxing option for skin laxity, wrinkles and acne scarring. Microneedling in general is a cosmetic procedure in which sterile needles repeatedly puncture the skin to induce a healing response, also called collagen induction therapy .
Evidence specific to Profound consists mainly of registered device studies run through ClinicalTrials.gov, including studies of cellulite cartridges, wrinkle and acne-scar usability testing, and a 500-person feasibility study of the Profound Matrix system . No peer-reviewed results are summarized here.

name: Secret RF

angle.text: Secret RF is used for skin quality and facial wrinkles through fractional microneedle radiofrequency. Two registered studies exist, with little else documented.

summary: Cutera's fractional microneedle RF device for skin quality and wrinkles, with two registered studies and little else documented here.
note: Thin documentation.
currentQuick:
Secret RF is a fractional radiofrequency microneedling device from Cutera, used in clinics for skin quality and facial wrinkles.
Two trials were registered in 2018; results are not summarized here.
How it works: Fine needles enter the skin and deliver RF energy in a fractional pattern, with the intended aim of stimulating remodeling.
Risks and caveats: Device-specific safety data are not covered here. General microneedling carries infection risk when performed without proper infection control.
deepLead:
Secret RF is a fractional microneedling radiofrequency device made by Cutera and used in aesthetic medicine for skin quality and facial wrinkles. Microneedling in general is a cosmetic procedure in which needles puncture the skin to prompt a healing response .
Published information available for this entry is limited to two clinical trial registrations.

name: Vivace RF microneedling

angle.text: Vivace is an RF microneedling device people consider for skin tightening and texture, in line with the wider RF microneedling category. No study located names the Vivace device itself.

summary: An RF microneedling aesthetic device; no study found that names Vivace itself.
note: No device-specific studies found.
currentQuick:
Vivace is an RF microneedling device offered in aesthetic clinics.
No device-specific study was located; only a trial of fractional microneedling RF as a category exists.
How it works: RF microneedling pairs needle punctures with radiofrequency energy intended to prompt skin remodeling.
Risks and caveats: Device-specific risks are not documented in the sources available. General microneedling infection concerns apply to procedures done without proper infection control.
deepLead:
Vivace is a radiofrequency microneedling device used in aesthetic procedures. No registered trial or published study located for this entry names the Vivace device specifically.
Microneedling generally is a cosmetic procedure in which sterile needles repeatedly puncture the skin; Wikipedia notes uses for scarring and acne . A registered 2023 trial compared facial muscle exercises with fractional microneedling radiofrequency, as a category, for facial aging .

name: Potenza RF

chain: Smoother skin, fewer scars and lines
angle.text: Potenza is used for wrinkles, fine lines, scars, stretch marks and pigmentation to improve skin quality. Evidence comes mainly from small registered studies.

summary: Cynosure's RF microneedling system for wrinkles, scars and pigmentation, documented mainly through small registered studies.
note: Outcome data not summarized from available sources.
currentQuick:
Potenza is a clinic-based RF microneedling system from Cynosure used for wrinkles, scars, stretch marks and pigmentation.
Available documentation is a handful of registered device studies with 8 to 79 participants.
How it works: Needles enter the skin and deliver radiofrequency energy intended to stimulate remodeling.
Risks and caveats: Device-specific safety findings are not summarized here. General microneedling infection concerns apply in unregulated settings.
deepLead:
Potenza is a radiofrequency microneedling system from Cynosure, used in aesthetic dermatology for wrinkles, fine lines, scars, stretch marks and pigmentation. Microneedling in general is a cosmetic procedure that punctures the skin with fine needles to induce healing .
Information is limited to registered device studies; outcome data are not summarized here.

name: Sofwave

angle.text: Sofwave is used for lifting the brow, neck and under-chin and softening fine lines, with minimal downtime. It is FDA-cleared, and a 2023 review describes clinically significant lift results across many registered trials.

summary: Needle-free ultrasound skin-lifting system with many registered trials; a 2023 review describes it as FDA-cleared with clinically significant lift results.
note: Expectation management is emphasized in the review.
currentQuick:
Sofwave uses ultrasound to heat the dermis, aiming to lift and tighten skin without needles. A 2023 review calls it FDA-cleared.
It has been registered in many studies for laxity, wrinkles, acne scars and cellulite; outcomes are not summarized here.
How it works: Ultrasound energy creates controlled thermal injury in dermal and subdermal tissue, leading to collagen remodeling.
Risks and caveats: Side effects are not detailed in the available sources; the review stresses patient selection and managing expectations.
deepLead:
Sofwave is an ultrasound-based, non-invasive skin-lifting system used in aesthetic medicine for skin laxity, wrinkles, acne scars and cellulite. A 2023 review describes ultrasound devices as delivering energy to dermal and subdermal tissue to cause thermal injury, leading to collagen remodeling and lifting, and lists Sofwave and Ulthera as FDA-cleared systems with clinically significant results for eyebrow, submental and neck lift and fine-line reduction .
Unlike RF microneedling, it does not involve needles. The review notes that patient selection and expectation management are important .

name: Ultherapy Prime

angle.text: Ultherapy Prime is the updated Ultherapy system, used for non-surgical lifting of the lower face and neck with improved imaging. Evidence for the original Ultherapy is broader; the Prime model itself is early-stage.

summary: Updated Ultherapy ultrasound lifting device with better imaging; evidence on the Prime model itself is still early-stage.
note: Prime-specific data are limited to early case series, a survey and a preprint.
currentQuick:
Ultherapy Prime is a newer version of the Ultherapy skin-lifting device. It uses focused ultrasound, guided by live imaging, to heat tissue beneath the skin at chosen depths.
It is used in clinics for brow, neck, under-chin and decolletage lifting. Published data on the Prime model are so far early case series and a survey.
How it works: Focused ultrasound creates tiny heat points in the deep dermis and fascia, which is reported to stimulate new collagen and elastin and a tightening effect.
Risks and caveats: A 2025 survey compared patient-reported pain, redness and swelling between Prime and the older system. Treatment is performed by clinicians; the MFU-V category is FDA-cleared for several body areas.
deepLead:
Ultherapy Prime is an updated version of the Ultherapy system, a noninvasive aesthetic device that uses microfocused ultrasound with real-time visualization (MFU-V) to tighten and lift skin. It is described in the literature as a second-generation system with an advanced processor and improved imaging compared with the original Ultherapy device.
Microfocused ultrasound delivers energy to tiny points at different depths of the skin, producing thermal coagulation that is said to trigger a wound-repair response and the formation of new collagen and elastin. A 2026 review states that MFU-V is cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration for brow lifting, neck and submental tightening and wrinkles of the decolletage, with additional clearance in 2025 for the abdomen and arms.
In looksmaxxing culture the procedure is grouped with non-surgical hardmaxxing options for jawline and neck definition. Published evidence on the Prime model specifically is limited to early case series, a patient survey and company-linked comparison data, as listed below.

name: Ulthera DeepSEE

angle.text: DeepSEE is used for non-surgical tightening of the lower face and under-chin, with imaging that lets the operator see tissue layers. A trial is registered but results are not summarised in available sources.

summary: Ulthera's imaging-guided ultrasound lifting system for the lower face and under-chin; trial registered, results not summarised in available sources.
note: Thin sources; model-specific results not available here.
currentQuick:
DeepSEE is an Ulthera ultrasound lifting system with built-in imaging, used by clinicians to tighten lax skin on the lower face and under the chin.
A 201-person study was registered and completed, but its results were not available in the sources reviewed.
How it works: Microfocused ultrasound delivers heat at set depths below the skin surface while imaging helps the operator see the target tissue.
Risks and caveats: Specific adverse-event data for this model were not available in the reviewed sources; MFU-V devices are discussed in the literature as noninvasive alternatives to surgery.
deepLead:
The Ulthera DeepSEE system is a microfocused ultrasound with visualization (MFU-V) device from Ulthera, used for noninvasive skin tightening of the lower face and submentum. Its name is tied to the imaging feature that lets the operator see tissue layers during treatment.
The main published evidence in the available sources is a registered, completed single-arm study of 201 participants evaluating effectiveness and safety for skin laxity of the lower face and submentum, and a consensus review of MFU-V use in Asian patients. Little community discussion of the specific model was found.

name: Doublo HIFU

angle.text: Doublo is a Korean HIFU device used for facial and neck skin tightening. Two small published studies in Asian patients have examined it.

summary: Korean HIFU skin-tightening device with two small published studies in Asian patients.
note: Evidence is limited to two small studies.
currentQuick:
Doublo is a Korean-made focused-ultrasound device used to tighten facial and neck skin.
Two small studies (11 and 43 patients) have been published; one authors' group described the technology as safe but of limited efficacy.
How it works: Focused ultrasound creates heat at various depths below the skin surface while sparing the surface layer.
Risks and caveats: The 2020 study describes IFUS as having a good safety profile; details beyond that were not available in the reviewed sources.
deepLead:
Doublo is an intense focused ultrasound (IFUS, also called HIFU) device made by HIRONIC Co. of Seongnam, Korea, used for noninvasive facial and neck skin tightening. Two published studies in Asian patients have examined it.
A 2015 study of 11 patients assessed histologic changes, safety and efficacy, and a 2020 prospective study of 43 patients reported the authors' experience treating neck and lower-face laxity. The latter paper describes IFUS as having a good safety profile but limited efficacy, with most earlier research having used the Ulthera system.

name: Ultraformer III

angle.text: Ultraformer III is a Korean HIFU device used for facial lifting and skin rejuvenation. Published studies are small and mostly cover the related Ultraformer MPT model.

summary: Korean HIFU lifting device; published studies are small and mostly cover the related Ultraformer MPT model.
note: Cited studies concern Ultraformer MPT rather than the III specifically.
currentQuick:
Ultraformer III is a Korean HIFU machine used in clinics for non-surgical facial lifting.
Published studies are small cohorts, mostly on the related Ultraformer MPT, covering facial lifting by area, eyelid sagging and ultrasound frequency.
How it works: Focused ultrasound heats tissue at selected depths, described as promoting collagen synthesis and reducing subcutaneous fat.
Risks and caveats: Safety details were not available beyond the studies' own safety evaluations; several larger device trials are registered.
deepLead:
Ultraformer III is a Korean high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) device used for noninvasive facial lifting and skin rejuvenation. Published studies in the sources cited here mainly concern the related Ultraformer MPT model, and are listed as such below.
HIFU is described as a noninvasive approach to facial rejuvenation reported to promote collagen synthesis and reduce subcutaneous fat. Studies have examined its effects by frequency, by facial aesthetic unit using 3D scanning, and on eyelid sagging.

name: Thermage FLX

angle.text: Thermage FLX is used for non-surgical tightening of the face, eye area and body. The Thermage line was the first monopolar RF skin-tightening system FDA-cleared, in 2002; evidence is many small studies and few controlled trials.

summary: In-office monopolar radiofrequency device for non-surgical skin tightening, backed by many small studies but few controlled trials.
note: Burns, scarring and fat loss have been reported with RF devices; results are described as lasting about one to two years.
currentQuick:
Thermage FLX is a clinic-based machine that uses monopolar radiofrequency energy to heat the deep skin layers. It is marketed for tightening lax skin and softening wrinkles on the face, neck and body without surgery.
Research consists largely of small studies, practitioner surveys and device-company-linked trials. Reports describe gradual, modest improvement over months, and several newer trials are registered.
How it works: Radiofrequency current is converted to heat by tissue resistance. The dermis is heated while surface cooling protects the epidermis; the heat is said to contract existing collagen and trigger new collagen formation over weeks to months.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include redness, swelling and pain, with burns, blistering, pigment change, dents, scarring and fat loss described less commonly. Pacemakers and pregnancy are listed contraindications. It is a clearance-regulated device used by trained clinicians.
deepLead:
Thermage FLX is a monopolar radiofrequency (RF) device used in aesthetic medicine to heat the deeper layers of the skin with the aim of tightening lax skin and reducing wrinkles without surgery. It is the latest generation of the Thermage line, which is described as the first monopolar RF skin-tightening system to receive US FDA clearance, for periorbital (eye-area) use in 2002 .
Radio-frequency skin tightening in general passes alternating current through tissue, which resists the current and converts it to heat; the dermis is heated while skin cooling protects the surface . Proponents and device makers say the heat causes immediate collagen contraction and later new collagen formation, with effects building over several months . Treatments are delivered by clinicians in office settings.
Published evidence on Thermage-type monopolar RF consists mainly of small, often single-arm, studies and clinician surveys, such as a questionnaire of 52 Korean dermatologists on the FLX version  and a 20-patient single-arm study of RF combined with fractional laser . Grokipedia notes that many studies are small and lack randomized controls . In forum culture, devices of this type are discussed as a non-surgical option for jawline and facial laxity.

name: Exilis Ultra / Exilis Elite

angle.text: Exilis is a BTL radiofrequency platform used on the face and body for non-surgical skin tightening. Little device-specific evidence appears in the sources reviewed.

summary: BTL's radiofrequency skin-tightening platform; discussed as a non-surgical option, with little device-specific evidence in the sources reviewed.
note: Device-specific published data were not found; category-wide RF risks include burns and scarring.
currentQuick:
Exilis is a BTL radiofrequency machine used in clinics for non-surgical skin tightening and body contouring. Ultra and Elite are newer versions of the platform.
The sources reviewed describe the RF category in general; model-specific trial data were not found.
How it works: Radiofrequency current is converted to heat in the skin, with the aim of contracting collagen and prompting new collagen over months.
Risks and caveats: Category reports include redness, swelling, pain, burns, blistering, pigment change and, less commonly, scarring or fat loss. Pacemakers and pregnancy are listed contraindications.
deepLead:
Exilis is a radiofrequency (RF) skin-tightening device line made by BTL, listed on Wikipedia among commercial RF devices for non-surgical skin tightening . Exilis Ultra and Exilis Elite are later versions of the platform, which is used by clinicians on the face and body.
RF skin tightening in general uses radiofrequency current converted to heat in tissue, with the aim of stimulating collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid and reducing lax skin and fine lines . Wikipedia describes RF devices as an alternative to facelifts and other surgery and notes uses on jowls, abdomen, thighs and arms, as well as cellulite and body contouring .
Published sources available for this article describe the device category rather than Exilis specifically, so detail on model-specific specifications, trial results and pricing is limited.

name: Venus Legacy

chain: RF plus magnetic fields and suction
angle.text: Venus Legacy is used for skin laxity, wrinkles, cellulite and mild fat reduction on the face and body. Published evidence is thin.

summary: Venus Concept's multipolar RF plus pulsed-magnetic-field device for skin tightening and contouring, with thin published evidence.
note: Evidence is limited to a short review and small registered studies.
currentQuick:
Venus Legacy is a clinic-based device from Venus Concept that combines radiofrequency, pulsed electromagnetic fields and suction. It is used for skin laxity, wrinkles and body contouring.
The published evidence found is a 2015 overview article and a couple of small registered studies.
How it works: Radiofrequency heats tissue to prompt collagen remodelling, with pulsed fields and suction added by the manufacturer's design.
Risks and caveats: Reported RF effects include redness, swelling, pain, burns and pigment change, and rarely scarring or fat loss. Pacemakers and pregnancy are listed contraindications.
deepLead:
Venus Legacy is a Venus Concept radiofrequency device for non-surgical skin tightening, wrinkle reduction and body contouring; Wikipedia lists it among commercial RF skin-tightening devices . Grokipedia describes it as a multipolar RF system that adds pulsed electromagnetic fields and pulsed suction, used for laxity, wrinkles, cellulite and mild fat reduction on the face and body .
A 2015 article in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology presented Venus Freeze and Venus Legacy as newer RF devices within the trend toward noninvasive skin tightening . Published evidence available for this article is limited to that review and small registered studies.

name: Venus Viva

angle.text: Venus Viva is used for acne scars, wrinkles and general resurfacing with shorter recovery than ablative approaches. Support comes from small uncontrolled studies.

summary: Nanofractional RF resurfacing device used for acne scars and wrinkles, supported by small uncontrolled studies.
note: Studies are small; fractional RF has downtime and burn/pigment risks.
currentQuick:
Venus Viva is a clinic device that delivers radiofrequency energy through tiny pins to resurface skin. It is used for acne scars, wrinkles and texture.
Published work is mainly small studies, including a 20-patient acne-scar study in darker skin types.
How it works: Fractional RF heats microscopic zones of skin through micro-pins, leaving surrounding tissue intact, which is described as shortening recovery.
Risks and caveats: Fractional resurfacing generally causes redness and swelling; burns and pigment change are reported RF risks. Sources reviewed provide little device-specific safety data.
deepLead:
Venus Viva is a nanofractional radiofrequency device marketed for skin resurfacing, including acne scars and wrinkles. Fractional RF delivers thermal energy through multiple micro-pins in a targeted pattern, which is described as shortening recovery compared with surgery or full ablation .
Evidence consists of small studies, including a 20-patient study of nanofractional RF for acne scars in Indian skin (Fitzpatrick types IV-V)  and a retrospective patient-satisfaction study , plus a number of small registered trials of fractional RF.

name: Pelleve

angle.text: Pellevé is used for wrinkle reduction and mild tightening, and followed Thermage as an RF option after 2002. Evidence comes from small uncontrolled studies.

summary: Ellman's 4-MHz monopolar RF system for wrinkles and tightening, backed by small uncontrolled studies.
note: Studies are small and mostly without control groups.
currentQuick:
Pellevé is a clinic-based monopolar radiofrequency system from Ellman International used for facial and neck wrinkles and, in one study, hand wrinkles.
Published work is limited to small studies of 12 to 31 patients.
How it works: Continuous 4-MHz radiofrequency energy heats skin to therapeutic temperature, with the aim of contracting collagen and stimulating new collagen.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed give little safety detail; category-wide RF reports include pain, burns, pigment change and rare scarring or fat loss.
deepLead:
Pellevé is a monopolar radiofrequency wrinkle-treatment system made by Ellman International, operating at 4 MHz . It was one of the RF devices that followed the introduction of Thermage in 2002 .
Published studies include a 17-patient facial study , a 31-patient hand-wrinkle study  and a 12-patient periorbital cohort . A 2011 clinical article describes the procedure as delivering continuous monopolar RF energy and repeatedly bringing skin to therapeutic temperatures until maximal contraction is obtained .

name: BodyTite

angle.text: BodyTite is used to remove fat while tightening the overlying skin, aiming at a leaner contour with less loose skin than liposuction alone. The visible contour change is the result of the procedure; evidence is mostly surgeon-reported series.

summary: InMode's radiofrequency-assisted liposuction that adds skin tightening to fat removal; evidence is mostly surgeon-reported series.
note: Reported risks include burns, infection, seroma and asymmetry; FDA clearance is for electrocoagulation and hemostasis.
currentQuick:
BodyTite is a radiofrequency-assisted liposuction system from InMode. It removes fat and uses heat in the tissue to encourage the skin to tighten, aimed at patients who have loose skin that liposuction alone may not address.
Published work consists mostly of surgeon-authored series and retrospective reviews, with small registered studies.
How it works: A subdermal probe delivers bipolar radiofrequency energy that liquefies fat and heats surrounding tissue, with temperature monitoring; the fat is then aspirated.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include swelling, bruising and numbness, with burns, infection, seroma, hematoma and asymmetry described as less common. A 97-patient series reported major complications in 6.25% of patients per one summary. US clearance covers electrocoagulation and hemostasis.
deepLead:
BodyTite is a radiofrequency-assisted liposuction (RFAL) system made by InMode. A probe placed beneath the skin delivers bipolar radiofrequency energy to liquefy fat and heat the tissue, after which the fat is aspirated; the heating is intended to make the skin contract, addressing laxity that liposuction alone may leave.
It is used for body areas such as the abdomen, flanks, arms and thighs, and published reports describe it as filling a treatment gap between liposuction and excisional surgery such as brachioplasty or abdominoplasty. Evidence consists mainly of surgeon-authored case series and retrospective reviews, with a small number of registered studies.
According to Grokipedia, the InMode RF System received US FDA 510(k) clearance (K163190) in December 2016 for electrocoagulation and hemostasis in dermatological and general surgical procedures, rather than for body contouring as such.

name: AccuTite

angle.text: AccuTite is used on the jowls and neck to reduce small fat deposits and tighten skin, for a more defined lower face with less downtime than a neck lift. Evidence is small studies and surgeon reviews.

summary: InMode's small-area radiofrequency-assisted lipolysis tool for jowl and neck tightening; evidence is small studies and surgeon reviews.
note: Minimally invasive procedure performed by clinicians; published data are small and surgeon-authored.
currentQuick:
AccuTite is a minimally invasive radiofrequency device from InMode that heats tissue under the skin to tighten it and reduce small fat deposits, mainly on the face and neck.
Surgeons present it as an option between noninvasive devices and a facelift. Published evidence is limited to small studies, case series and reviews.
How it works: Radiofrequency energy is delivered into the subdermal space to heat dermal collagen and fat. Reviews describe this as targeting skin laxity and adipose tissue together.
Risks and caveats: Reviews describe lower risk than revision facelifts, but no detailed complication rates for AccuTite appear in the available literature reviewed, and studies are small.
deepLead:
AccuTite is a minimally invasive radiofrequency-assisted lipolysis device from InMode, used for small-area skin tightening and fat reduction, typically on the face and neck. Published reports describe it, together with FaceTite, as delivering radiofrequency energy into the subdermal space to target dermal collagen and excess fat with less downtime and lower cost than open procedures such as neck lifts.
Surgeon-authored papers describe a so-called treatment gap of patients whose laxity is too great for noninvasive devices but not severe enough, or not desired, for a facelift. The evidence consists of small registered studies, case series and review articles.

name: Vaser liposuction

angle.text: VASER is used for body contouring and abs "etching", where fat removal around muscle shows more definition. The change is visible once healed; evidence is mostly surgeon case series and a few small trials.

summary: Ultrasound-assisted liposuction used for body contouring and abs 'etching'; evidence is mostly surgeon case series plus a few small trials.
note: Surgical procedure; liposuction carries risks including infection, bleeding and embolism.
currentQuick:
VASER is a brand of ultrasound-assisted liposuction. It uses ultrasonic energy to loosen fat before it is suctioned out and is widely associated with high-definition liposculpture, which aims to show muscle outlines such as the abdominals.
Published work is largely surgeon-reported case series, with a few small comparative trials against conventional suction liposuction.
How it works: A probe delivers ultrasonic energy into the fat layer, and the fat is then aspirated. Surgeons describe work on superficial fat as the basis of definition procedures.
Risks and caveats: Liposuction in general carries reported risks including infection, bleeding, blood clots, organ perforation and fat embolism, with risk rising with volume removed. A dedicated review covers complications of high-definition liposculpture.
deepLead:
VASER (vibration amplification of sound energy at resonance) liposuction is a form of ultrasound-assisted liposuction in which a probe delivers ultrasonic energy to fat before it is suctioned out. It is described in the surgical literature as a third-generation ultrasound technique, introduced after earlier ultrasound devices that surgeons reported as bulky and associated with a higher potential for complications.
In appearance culture it is best known as the tool behind high-definition liposculpture, sometimes called abdominal etching, in which fat is removed or shaped to emphasise the outline of muscle groups such as the abdominals. Surgeons who developed the approach reported using VASER to treat superficial fat layers and to define musculature as well as to reduce volume.
Published evidence consists mainly of surgeon-reported case series and a small number of comparative trials against conventional suction-assisted liposuction. Liposuction in general is described as removing fat locally without producing lasting weight loss.

name: Power-assisted liposuction (PAL)

angle.text: PAL is a motorized liposuction variant users consider for removing stubborn fat in a smoother, more precise way. The contour change is visible after healing; the claimed precision advantage has little head-to-head trial evidence.

summary: A motorized, vibrating-cannula version of liposuction; documented in surgical reports but with little head-to-head trial evidence.
note: Surgical procedure; carries general liposuction risks.
currentQuick:
Power-assisted liposuction uses a cannula driven by a motor so it vibrates while moving through fat. It is a variant of ordinary liposuction used for body contouring, male chest reduction and fat harvesting.
Published work is mostly surgeons describing their technique. Few randomized comparisons with conventional liposuction exist.
How it works: A motorized handpiece moves the suction cannula rapidly back and forth, which proponents say reduces manual effort for the surgeon and eases passage through fat. It is typically paired with tumescent anesthetic solution.
Risks and caveats: As an operation, it shares liposuction risks reported in the literature, including pain, bruising, contour irregularities, infection, bleeding and clots, with rare deaths; risk is reported to increase with volume removed.
deepLead:
Power-assisted liposuction (PAL) is a variant of suction lipectomy in which the cannula is driven by a motor so that it vibrates or reciprocates rapidly while the surgeon moves it through subcutaneous fat. It is one of several liposuction techniques, alongside tumescent, ultrasound-assisted, laser-assisted and water-jet-assisted methods.
Proponents of the technique say the mechanical motion lets surgeons remove fat with less manual effort, and it has been described in published surgical reports for body contouring, superficial liposuction, gynecomastia in men and fat harvesting for grafting. In looksmaxxing communities it is mentioned mainly as a body-contouring option within the broader category of liposuction.
Published evidence consists mostly of surgeons' case series and small comparative studies; few randomized trials compare PAL with conventional suction-assisted liposuction, and the procedure is a surgical operation with the same general risk categories as other forms of liposuction.

name: Water-assisted liposuction (BodyJet)

angle.text: Water-assisted liposuction, including the BodyJet system, is used for fat removal and body contouring. The contour change is visible after healing; documentation is mainly for fat harvesting, with thinner contouring data.

summary: Liposuction using a pressurized fan-shaped water jet; documented mainly for fat harvesting, with thin evidence for contouring outcomes.
note: Surgical procedure; carries general liposuction risks.
currentQuick:
Water-assisted liposuction uses a jet of fluid to loosen fat while it is suctioned out. BodyJet is a branded system. It is used for body contouring and for collecting fat to transfer elsewhere.
Published studies are mostly fat-grafting case series and lab comparisons, not contouring trials.
How it works: A fan-shaped water jet through the cannula delivers fluid and anesthetic and detaches fat, which is then aspirated.
Risks and caveats: Risks are those of liposuction generally, including pain, bruising, contour irregularity, infection, bleeding, clots and rare deaths. No device-specific safety data were identified.
deepLead:
Water-assisted liposuction (WAL), also called water-jet-assisted liposuction, is a liposuction technique in which a fan-shaped jet of fluid is delivered through the cannula to loosen fat and infiltrate anesthetic while the fat is aspirated. BodyJet is a commercial system for the method.
The technique is used for body contouring and for harvesting fat for transfer to other areas such as the breast. Published research on the method is concentrated in fat-grafting and tissue-quality studies rather than in appearance outcomes of contouring.

name: Tumescent liposuction

chain: Dilute lidocaine numbs and swells fat
angle.text: Tumescent liposuction is the standard technique for removing localized fat under local anesthesia, used on areas such as the abdomen, flanks, neck and jowls. The contour change is visible after healing; safety data come from large surgeon surveys.

summary: Liposuction under local anesthesia using large volumes of dilute lidocaine; the standard technique, with safety data from large surgeon surveys.
note: Lidocaine toxicity is the technique-specific concern reported in the literature.
currentQuick:
Tumescent liposuction fills fat with dilute numbing solution before suction, so patients can stay awake under local anesthesia. It was developed by dermatologists in the 1980s and is now a standard technique.
Large surveys of dermatologic surgeons have examined its safety, and studies report good long-term results in lipedema.
How it works: Lidocaine numbs the tissue and epinephrine narrows blood vessels, reducing bleeding and bruising while fat is aspirated through thin cannulas.
Risks and caveats: The literature reports lidocaine toxicity as a concern, plus general liposuction risks such as infection, bleeding, clots and contour irregularity. A 1999 report noted deaths and that reporting is not mandatory, so incidence is uncertain.
deepLead:
Tumescent liposuction is a liposuction technique in which large volumes of dilute lidocaine and epinephrine are infiltrated into subcutaneous fat before fat is aspirated through thin cannulas. The solution numbs the area and constricts blood vessels to reduce bleeding, so the procedure can be done under local anesthesia. It is credited to dermatologist Jeffrey Klein in the 1980s.
It is a standard approach to body contouring and is also used for lipedema. Safety data come largely from surveys of dermatologic surgeons; a 1999 analysis of deaths and surveys of tens of thousands of procedures have been published, and the main specific concern discussed in the literature is lidocaine dosing.
